t: #2584 Split the Array to Make Coprime Products
o: A split after index i is valid iff no prime divides elements on both sides. So for each prime p appearing anywhere, find its last occurrence index; a split at i is valid iff every prime occurring in the prefix nums[0..i] has its last occurrence <= i. Scan i left to right maintaining the maximum last-occurrence among primes seen so far; the first i (with i <= n-2) where that maximum equals i is the answer. Products themselves are astronomically large, hence the prime-based reformulation. Example [4,7,8,15,3,5]: prime 2 last occurs at index 2, so splits at 0,1 fail; at i=2 the prefix primes {2,7} all end at <= 2 — valid.
k: Work with prime factors, not products: gcd(prefix, suffix) > 1 iff some prime spans both sides.
For each distinct prime, only its last occurrence index matters.
One left-to-right scan tracking max(last occurrence) finds the earliest valid split.

a.i: Precompute each number's distinct primes and each prime's last index; sweep maintaining the running maximum of last indices.
s: Trial-divide each nums[i] into its distinct primes; record last[p] = i.
Sweep i from 0 to n-2, updating mx = max(mx, last[p]) for each prime p of nums[i].
If mx <= i, return i; after the loop return -1.
a.t: O(n * sqrt(A)) for trial division (A <= 1e6), plus O(total primes) for the sweeps
a.sp: O(n + P) where P is the number of distinct primes

w: Never multiply the numbers — they overflow instantly. Edge case: n = 1 has no valid split (loop doesn't run, returns -1). A sieve of smallest prime factors speeds factorization if values were larger. Follow-up: return all valid splits instead of the first.
